title: Prove there is no look-ahead: the truncation test

explain.prompt: The quant team says: “our features are fine, we used merge_asof.” In 4–6 sentences with your results: what the truncation test checks, which builders fail and why, why one cutoff is not enough, and why the 10-day target of 3.5 is allowed to fail it.
rubric: A truncation test rebuilds the features from the database as it looked at a cutoff (reports published by then, prices settled by then) and compares them with the full build on the common dates: any difference means a past row used information from after the cutoff.
The correct builder (backward join on availability, trailing 52-report average) changes 0 of 878 rows at the 27 June 2022 cutoff.

Standardising the surprise with the full-sample standard deviation changes 868 of 878 rows: a single global statistic contaminates every row. The centred 52-week average changes 123 rows (from 29 Dec 2021): it uses the 26 reports that come after each date.

The week_ending join changes 6 rows at the Monday cutoff (from 17 June 2022) but 0 at the Thursday cutoff three days later: a join-key leak only shows when the cutoff falls between the end of a week and its publication. Test several cutoffs, including the eve of releases.

Labels are different: the 10-day forward return is supposed to use future prices; it is handled by purging (only rows whose target was realised before the estimation origin are used, 3.6), not by the truncation test.
merge_asof is necessary but not sufficient: the leaks here come from a wrong key, a global statistic and a centred window — all compatible with 'we used merge_asof'.
